title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
abstract: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about 100times PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At 594times and 1,002times PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about 100times PLE compression. During inference at about 100times PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.

title: AgenticEvolve: Evolutionary Program Search with Persistent Language Model Agents that Design and Run Experiments
abstract: Evolutionary program search with large language models keeps the structure of an evolutionary algorithm and uses the model as its variation operator. Typically, the model generates each candidate program in a single request from parent programs and their scores. We present AgenticEvolve, an evolutionary program search framework in which each island is run by a persistent large language model agent. Between evaluations, the agent designs and runs experiments on the candidate program. To measure the contribution of experimentation, we compare AgenticEvolve with No-analysis, an otherwise identical configuration with experiments disabled. On two heuristic design tasks with three large language models, AgenticEvolve produces better programs than No-analysis and OpenEvolve on both hidden and unseen instances. It reaches the baselines'final quality with far fewer evaluations and comparable cost. On twelve equation discovery problems, it recovers the ground-truth structure of more equations than No-analysis and existing language-model and genetic programming baselines.

title: A Task-Centric Survey of Long-Document Visual Question Answering: Taxonomy, Evolution, and Future Directions
abstract: Visual document understanding is essential for acquiring knowledge from visually rich documents and is attracting growing research interest. Existing surveys emphasize architectures or technical approaches, with limited attention to how task bottlenecks shape technical choices and research priorities. We present a task-centric survey that decomposes long-document visual question answering (VQA) into four components: document parsing, evidence organization and retrieval, generator organization and learning, and evaluation. For each, we develop a fine-grained taxonomy and trace motivations, technical responses, and cross-component connections. We focus on explicit retrieval while covering direct reading. Our temporal analysis traces expanding priorities from multimodal content understanding to sufficient, high-fidelity evidence acquisition and sustained evidence management. We outline future directions in evidence sufficiency, verifiable and correctable understanding, and budget-aware coordination, with an outlook on continual document understanding.

title: AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark
abstract: AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses sim10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.

title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
abstract: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.

title: HiP3R: Hierarchical Pose Graphs for Long-Horizon 3D Reconstruction
abstract: Feed-forward models accurately estimate camera motion and 3D geometry from short video windows. However, computational and memory costs prevent direct inference on sequences containing thousands of frames. Long videos must therefore be processed as overlapping chunks. This division produces independent local reconstructions with inconsistent coordinate frames and duplicate estimates of shared cameras. Achieving global consistency requires propagating constraints from adjacent overlaps and distant revisits across the sequence. This requirement naturally motivates pose graph optimization. However, the choice of graph level creates a trade-off. Chunk-level graphs efficiently resolve scale drift and close large loops. Yet, their rigid transformations cannot correct internal errors or conflicting frame predictions. Conversely, frame-level optimization offers local flexibility, but scaling it globally is computationally expensive and can break metric scale. HiP3R resolves this trade-off using a hierarchical pose graph. HiP3R first optimizes a robust chunk-level Sim(3) graph to establish the global layout and scale. It then holds this layout fixed and estimates one shared SE(3) camera per frame, turning overlapping window predictions into a single trajectory. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of HiP3R in improving camera trajectories and 3D reconstruction. Our method applies to both chunk-based and streaming backends without additional training or fine-tuning. The codes are available at https://kkakkkka.github.io/HiP3R.

title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.

title: PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?
abstract: Automated research is largely evaluated by benchmark performance, but the value of research rarely reduces to a single score. Humans judge a work's holistic contribution through peer review, which is hard to model because it is noisy and depends on many factors. However, what if, given only the paper, we could predict its peer-review decision directly? We introduce PaperScorer, a family of models that predict a paper's accept or reject decision from its extracted text or page screenshots, training only on the decision after removing author identity and formatting shortcuts. Vision models are the most predictive (68% accuracy on ICLR papers and 77% on ML papers from arXiv), beating text-only and frontier reasoning models. Unlike plain text, page images retain figures, layout, and presentation. This signal is robust, surviving smaller models and even compressing the whole paper into a single image. But accurate predictions are not evenly spread. PaperScorer is strongest on the lowest and highest rated papers, while papers rated in the middle stay unpredictable for our models and frontier systems alike. Additionally, its confidence is calibrated, so its most confident predictions are also its most accurate. Overall, PaperScorer shows how much of the decision a paper carries on its own, marking a first step toward AI-driven research evaluation.

title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning
abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi-layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well-suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma-Lab-Berkeley/Nestor .

title: DraMaze: A Multi-Agent Pipeline with Future-Aware Memory for Diverse Microdrama Script Generation
abstract: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.

title: Pairing Matters: Performance, Failures, and Efficiency in Lightweight Coding Agents
abstract: Self-hosting coding agents is often necessary for software-engineering teams that must keep proprietary code and development traces within controlled infrastructure. Lightweight, open-weight models make such deployment more feasible by reducing hardware requirements, while strong results on repository-level benchmarks demonstrate their potential for demanding coding tasks. Deploying these models as coding agents requires pairing them with an agent harness, making their joint performance a key deployment consideration. Yet existing leaderboards primarily report fixed harness-model configurations rather than controlled comparisons across alternative pairings. To address this gap, we investigate harness-model interactions through a controlled full-factorial evaluation of six open-source harnesses and three lightweight coding models across 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, producing 1,800 graded runs under common serving, metering, and grading conditions. For the same model, resolution rates differ by up to 44 percentage points across harnesses, while harness rankings change across models. We apply an evidence-based failure taxonomy to 1,100 unsuccessful runs and find substantial differences in failure patterns across harness-model pairings. A model's dominant failure modes under one harness need not dominate under another. Efficiency is similarly dependent on the pairing: even among model-directed loop harnesses, charged tokens per resolved task vary by more than 20-fold. These findings make harness-model selection a central deployment decision for lightweight coding agents. Strong performance with one harness or model does not guarantee similar results with another. We translate these findings into practitioner guidance for pairing selection, token-efficiency assessment, and trajectory-informed harness engineering, and release the complete experimental records and analysis artifacts.

title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.

title: OpenDraco: A Platform for Engineering and Experimenting with Configurable Multi-Agent Architectures for Software Engineering
abstract: Experimenting with LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) involves an iterative cycle of modeling configurations, executing and evaluating them, comparing results, and refining system designs. Existing approaches provide limited end-to-end support for this experimentation lifecycle. We present OpenDraco, an open-source platform that integrates these activities into a single workflow. OpenDraco represents agents, prompts, tools, models, parameters, and communication topology in exportable, versioned JSON specifications, translated into executable LangGraph workflows supporting different interaction structures. Users can modify and re-evaluate configurations using local or cloud-based LLMs. We instantiate OpenDraco for automated program repair (APR) and evaluate a sequential baseline and seven reconstructed configurations on synthetic and real-world SWE-bench Lite issues. The results reveal substantial cost differences among configurations with similar repair outcomes, while the baseline resolves 12 of 77 SWE-bench issues using open-source LLMs. Additional proof-of-concept tasks illustrate applicability beyond APR. OpenDraco supports iterative experimentation with heterogeneous MAS configurations, enabling researchers to examine their outcomes and costs within a common environment. Demonstration video: https://youtu.be/278sOR4lBEk.

title: CausalOdyssey: Multi-Agent Local LLM Reasoning with Per-Patient Causal Structure for Rare Disease Retrieval
abstract: Patients with rare diseases often wait years for a diagnosis. Existing HPO-based retrieval tools narrow the differential to a shortlist, but a clinician reading that shortlist has no signal for which candidate to trust or what to test next. We present CausalOdyssey, a local four-agent pipeline on Gemma 4 26B built over a classical IC-weighted gene-rescue backbone: a Diagnostician reranks the slate via chain-of-thought over per-patient FCI causal edges and Reactome mechanism context; a Verifier computes deterministic evidence against the top-1 (missing pathognomonic phenotypes, pathway chain closure) and has Gemma issue a confirm/flag/refute verdict over it; an Interrogator selects one follow-up HPO by split-variance scoring; a Narrator emits citation-validated clinical prose. Only the Diagnostician changes the ranking; the other three agents annotate it. On RareBench n=1,122, reranking a top-30 slate lifts R@1 by +12.57 pp over our structural baseline ([+10.07, +14.97]; p=8.3e-24). A no-LLM variant of that baseline, without its inverse disease-count weight, reaches a similar pooled R@1 (36.3% vs 35.3%): the LLM rerank is far better on metabolic cases (RAMEDIS, +16.0 pp) and far worse on case-report corpora (LIRICAL, MME), so its value is corpus-dependent. We also propose a masked-phenotype protocol for evaluating follow-up suggestions without an annotation-based oracle; under it, the Interrogator asks for a patient's hidden phenotypes no more often than simple baselines (0.6% vs 1.2%), although a perfect follow-up would add 11 pp at top-1. The Verifier's verdict separates correct from incorrect top-1s (51.4% vs 12.1% top-1 accuracy under confirm vs refute). For 30% of patients the gold diagnosis is outside our top-30, though LIRICAL retrieves over half of these. All inference is local; no patient data leaves the machine. Demo code and a live demo are public.

title: SUDO: From Scientific Publications to Global Scholarly Discourse
abstract: Scholarly Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) support literature search, scientific discovery, and agent-assisted research. Yet, most approaches to SKG construction pre-specify the knowledge unit to be represented, typically named scholarly entities or contribution-level statements, and retain only the publication content expressible through that unit. This choice produces two dominant yet distinct paradigms: concept-centric SKGs that preserve entities and local relations, and statement-centric SKGs that capture high-level discourse in sentences. In both cases, the graph reflects a chosen extraction target rather than how a paper constructs and communicates knowledge. We introduce SUDO, the Scholarly Upper Discourse Ontology, which defines how knowledge elements are organized and related to form a paper's research narrative, namely its scholarly discourse. Using linguistic principles that generalize across fields and tasks, SUDO enables each publication's scholarly discourse to be constructed from the bottom up as a coherent, source-grounded representation. Applied consistently across papers, the same structure connects their research narratives into a global scholarly discourse without discarding local context or provenance. We demonstrate SUDO's capabilities across a comprehensive suite of scholarly knowledge-modeling use cases and performance improvements on a downstream Large Language Model (LLM)-based scientific QA task.

title: Physiology as Topology: Intervenable Organ Graphs for Longitudinal Patient Forecasting
abstract: Do language models forecast patient trajectories by reasoning through physiology, or by fitting surface statistics? We introduce PhysioCircuit, a multi-agent agent system that represents each organ as an agent and each physiological relation as an editable mechanism card with direction, lag, and evidence. Its expert-defined graph is frozen at inference, enabling controlled edge interventions. We also introduce PhysioCircuit-Bench, a mechanism-controlled benchmark spanning three organ systems, treatment events, and real ICU admissions. We evaluate intervention-direction agreement (IDAR), which requires the affected organ to change in the expected direction within the expected lag window. The expert graph substantially outperforms all topology controls on edge-IDAR, including fully connected, random, and reversed graphs. Independent clinician adjudication supports the counterfactual results. PhysioCircuit transfers to new organ systems by configuration alone, without retraining, while preserving inspectable and editable relations.

title: WorldCast: World-Consistent Character Video Generation with Large-Angle Camera Control
abstract: Precise camera control is essential for cinematic character video generation, yet existing methods struggle to follow large-angle trajectories with combined rotation, translation, and radius variation from arbitrary initial azimuths. Such viewpoint changes also reveal character regions unseen in the initial frame, causing geometric distortions, appearance degradation, and identity drift. To systematically study these coupled challenges, we introduce CLACT, a large-scale Character-centric dataset and benchmark covering diverse Large-Angle Camera Trajectories, with accurate camera geometry and multi-view character observations for training and evaluation. We further propose WorldCast, a framework for world-consistent character video generation under diverse large-angle camera motions. Specifically, we back-project the initial frame into a 3D point cloud using estimated depth, align the point-cloud scale with the target camera trajectory, and render it along the trajectory to obtain explicit geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement the incomplete character information, we introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using relative camera poses estimated jointly from the initial frame and multi-view character anchors, we express anchor and target-view geometry in a common coordinate frame. GAMA uses this geometric alignment to guide the retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features during generation. Evaluations across diverse large-angle camera trajectories demonstrate accurate trajectory following while preserving character geometry, appearance, and identity.

title: World-in-Context: Interactive Video World Modeling with In-Context Conditioning
abstract: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM (81.5 vs. 81.6) and attains a 93.8% perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines (18.8%). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts.

title: NewsBench: Expert-Grounded Evaluation of Epistemic Quality in AI News Reporting
abstract: As frontier AI systems increasingly serve as sources of political and current-events information, evaluating the epistemic quality of their responses is now especially consequential. Existing evaluations often focus narrowly on ideological alignment, rely on measures not validated for this setting, or depend on reference labels derived from public opinion or non-expert annotation, potentially producing misleading or miscalibrated results. To address these limitations, we introduce NewsBench, an expert-grounded benchmark that reframes evaluation around editorial standards developed by senior practitioners in journalism, policy, and intelligence analysis. NewsBench operationalizes quality across three dimensions, source quality, factuality, and neutrality, using a two-phase pipeline in which domain experts first define and calibrate evaluation guidelines, which are then transferred to automated AI judges validated against expert-adjudicated gold labels. The benchmark includes approximately $3,000$ evaluation prompts, with roughly $500$ refreshed monthly to capture emerging current events, roughly $2,500$ human expert-annotated items for calibration and validation, and a suite of AI judges designed to enable scalable evaluation. To validate our methodology, we report both inter-rater reliability among human experts and AI judge--human agreement across all three dimensions. Finally, we apply NewsBench to four frontier models, revealing distinct and non-overlapping failure profiles in sourcing, factuality, and neutrality.

title: RadonBench: A Benchmark of Classical and Learning-Guided Search Techniques for Problems in Combinatorial Geometry
abstract: Classical optimization and learning-guided search offer complementary approaches to open problems in discrete mathematics, but their outputs are difficult to compare when search spaces, validity checks, and stopping rules differ. We present \emph{RadonBench}, a benchmark for constructing maximum-cardinality Radon-free lattice configurations: finite subsets of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ admitting no integral Radon partition. It remains open whether Radon-free configurations with $11$ points in $\mathbb{Z}^3$ or $21$ points in $\mathbb{Z}^4$ are possible. If they exist, they would improve the corresponding lower bounds on the integer Radon numbers. We compare exhaustive extension, greedy local search, PatternBoost, AlphaZero, and AlphaEvolve. All outputs use one success predicate: a convex target-sized configuration succeeds exactly when its number of integral Radon points is zero. PatternBoost and AlphaZero construct verified Radon-free configurations of sizes $10$ and $20$, one point short of the respective targets; AlphaZero's best convex target terminals have two integral Radon points in both dimensions. Exhaustive extension over fixed seeds and declared finite search boxes likewise reaches a minimum of two integral Radon points. Greedy local search and AlphaEvolve each produce target-sized near misses with one integral Radon point. No audited run reaches zero. These results establish reproducible near-miss baselines over explicitly scoped search domains.

title: AgentOrch: How Close Can Global Orchestration Come to Step-by-Step Interaction?
abstract: Enterprise workflow agents typically rely on step-by-step interaction (Step-by-Step): the agent executes an action, observes its result, and invokes a large language model (LLM) again to decide the next step. Global orchestration (Global) instead generates a complete executable workflow in advance and executes it without further LLM calls, substantially reducing inference overhead, but it remains less accurate than Step-by-Step. We study how close Global can come to Step-by-Step and what narrows the remaining gap. We introduce AgentOrch, a benchmark that directly compares global orchestration with step-by-step interaction on 650 enterprise SOPs and 3,220 runtime variants under matched tools, environments, and evaluation. Step-by-Step remains more accurate for every evaluated model, but the gap has shrunk by about 79% from early models to the strongest recent model. We identify three routes to further narrowing this gap. Incremental workflow construction improves Global accuracy by an average of 9.98 percentage points (pp) without runtime execution feedback. Revising complete workflows with execution feedback improves all evaluated models, including 6.13 pp on held-out runtime variants. Targeted training on complete workflows improves accuracy by an average of 12.18 pp across all five trained models. Although a gap remains, global orchestration offers a promising path toward enterprise agents that deliver higher accuracy with fewer LLM calls.

title: Secure and Functional Code Generation with Self-Evaluation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code that remains insecure. Security-focused fine-tuning can be expensive and is not always available, motivating inference-time approaches. Security-oriented prompting and retrieval can reduce vulnerabilities, but may also remove required behavior or apply defenses incompatible with the task. The challenge is to identify relevant security knowledge and use it to improve security without sacrificing functionality. We present SecGent, an inference-time framework that retrieves weakness context from the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) database and applies it to secure code generation. By connecting task specifications to relevant textual CWE records, SecGent provides task-specific security guidance without relying on retrieved vulnerable or patched code examples. Complementary functional and security tests check the resulting implementation, and their execution feedback guides repairs toward satisfying both objectives. We evaluate SecGent with four open-source LLMs and Claude Sonnet 5.5 across five programming languages on the CWEval benchmark. It achieves the highest joint functional--security success against four inference-time baselines for all five models. Across the open-weight models, mean functional-security@1 (FS@1) improves by 15.5% over RAG, with gains in both functionality and security, and by 19.8% over the strongest prompt optimizer compiled for each model. On Sonnet, FS@1 reaches 92.1%, outperforming the strongest baseline AutoGen by 4.8%. In a separate comparison, SecGent outperforms Claude Code with security-focused prompting by over 6% in FS@1. Feedback-guided repair further improves FS@1 by up to 6.7% over generation without feedback, primarily by recovering functionality while checking security.

title: PACE: Research Proving Agent for Adaptive Conjecture Exploration
abstract: Many mathematical research agents focus on solving problems with fixed statements. However, conjecture research, especially in applied mathematics, may require revising candidate questions or conclusions as investigation proceeds, coupling problem formulation with proof development. We present PACE, a research-proof agent that supports this process through a structured research loop that selects mathematical objectives and develops or challenges candidate mechanisms. The whole prover constructs proofs from these mechanisms, and an independent verifier checks them against the original target. Evidence-tracking memory stores assumptions and dependencies arising during research and marks evidence for revalidation when a candidate or condition changes. This memory supports task-specific context composition that keeps checked premises, exploratory material and unresolved obligations distinct. To evaluate proof construction and conjecture research, we introduce ResearchProofBench, an applied-mathematics benchmark focused on optimization, comprising 51 known-proof tasks with 331 hidden checkpoints under historical abstract access and six open-problem cases. The known-proof tasks assess reconstruction of published results, while the open-problem cases assess mathematical investigation and proof development. On the 51 known-proof tasks, PACE achieves an aggregate Proof Score of 75.16 and completes 20 proofs. In conjecture research, PACE develops conditional results, with its submissions receiving higher review scores than the compared baselines.

title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
abstract: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

title: Beyond Benchmarks: Can Small Open-Weight Models Get Real Coding Work Done?
abstract: Making an open-weight language model generate text is not the same as making it finish coding work. This retrospective empirical systems experience report follows my engineering work from July to October 2026 across coding clients, model-specific serving recipes, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, and MLX. Models behind a nominally compatible endpoint still differed in tool-call formatting, turn control, context behavior, cache reuse, and reliability. A served model, coherent text, executed tool calls, and code that passes independent behavioral checks proved to be distinct levels of progress. The evidence includes 4,165 coding-agent gateway turns from my own sessions, 623 debug jobs, and three separate delegation studies with hidden behavioral checks and a fixed Claude Opus 5.5 parent. Saved cold-prefix requests had a median time to first token of about 69.4 s, versus 2.8 s for high-reuse requests (observational). In a 45-trial study, direct coding passed 15/15 and delegation to a quantized Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B worker passed 12/15 and 14/15. On a second 15-task suite under a fixed artifact contract, the completed replacement cohort had 45/45 for direct coding and 12/45 for a Nemotron Cascade 2 worker (11 worker substitutions). Sixteen sessions stopped by a subscription limit before any model call were replaced; counting them as failures gives 37/45 and 8/45. A Qwen3-Coder worker passed 0/45. In both studies with a direct arm, direct coding had lower API list-price-equivalent frontier cost per verified success. A post-hoc diagnostic found that 19 of 36 artifacts rejected only for renamed parameters passed the hidden checks unchanged; they are not counted as successes. The contribution is an evidence-qualified account of serving, agent protocol, session continuity, artifact validation, and verification in practice. The studies are not pooled and do not rank models or runtimes.

title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration
abstract: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.

title: More Memory, Better Videos? A Controlled Study of Visual Memory in Long-Video Generation
abstract: Long-video generators increasingly retrieve past visual observations to prevent identity drift. The intuition is compelling: more access to history should make future video more consistent. But an image can be faithful to the past and wrong for the present. Does visual memory always improve the generated story? We investigate this question through VMem-Bench, a two-track diagnostic study. Track-A measures which references are selected from 92 real films (16,548 segments), before generation and without generator confounds. Track-B compares four retrieval policies with no-memory and gold-informed last-seen controls on 30 causally generated stories (2,824 segments) using a shared generator. Retrieval increases entity recall from 0.559 to 0.628-0.693 and improves similarity to past appearances, but decreases precision from 0.977 to 0.915-0.938 and forbidden-entity avoidance from 0.968 to 0.845-0.898. It can also reinforce obsolete appearances after the story changes them. Conversely, high long-gap recall can arise without memory when the prompt itself supplies the appearance; an appearance-stripping analysis exposes this confound. These results distinguish historical fidelity from current-story correctness and show why retrieval relevance or final-video consistency alone does not establish memory utility.

title: Ask Before You Answer: A Question-Driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture (QERA) for In-Context Learning
abstract: AI assistants are increasingly asked to reason over a user's own web traces: group chats, community threads, activity logs and revision histories. On CL-bench Life, a benchmark of such real-life context learning, frontier LLMs solve fewer than one task in five. We find that the request is not the specification: over 80% of the benchmark's rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request, as for a rule set two turns earlier or every record that meets the user's criterion, and LLMs answering directly pass only 67% of these implicit rubrics against 81% of the others. We propose QERA, a Question-driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture that asks before it answers. QERA first turns the request into a requirement checklist and typed information needs, filtered by code for faithfulness to the user's words; it then answers from the whole conversation, asks the same questions again with quotes verified by code, and applies a guarded local repair. It needs no training or rubrics and makes about four LLM calls per task. On all 405 tasks with four frontier LLMs, QERA attains the highest solving rate on every LLM (21.0% on average, against 18.2% for the strongest of three inference-time baselines and 14.6% for direct answering) and leads every baseline significantly when pooled across LLMs, while using fewer tokens than PSCI and 4-5% of the tokens of Ctx2Skill. Ablations on GPT-6-Luna show that the gain is settled before the answer, by a fixed answer protocol (+3.8 rubric points) and the request-specific questions (+1.6), and that it is concentrated on implicit rubrics, with checking afterwards refining mainly numeric requirements.

title: RepoTrace: Improving Requirement Tracing in Multi-Round Agent Interactions
abstract: Code agents have become increasingly capable of performing software engineering tasks through interaction with software environments. However, agents tend to degrade as the number of interaction rounds increases, making it difficult to maintain existing software during iterative modification. We analyze 2,656 agent trajectories in EvoCode-Bench and identify requirement focus misalignment as a recurring failure pattern, where agents struggle to distinguish the primary modification targets of a requirement from unrelated code. We propose Repotrace a requirement-driven repository understanding harness that combines repository structure with requirement semantics to construct a requirement-code correspondence and injects it into the agent context. This correspondence enables code agents to follow the repository architecture, trace requirements across multi-round interactions, and identify the core code elements corresponding to the current requirement. Experiments show that Repotrace improves the mean per-round reward (MPR) across different models (e.g., +19.99 on GLM-5.2) and agent harnesses (e.g., +10.22 on Claude Code). Across rounds, Repotrace increases the average per-round reward from 0.163 to 0.371 on Terminus-2 with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, while reducing average regression errors by 56.78%. We release the source code and agents'trajectories to support future research.

title: Toward Evidence-Based Agentic Software Engineering
abstract: Task success rates and execution costs of agentic coding tools depend on both model and harness. The harness manages context, provides tools, and runs the agent loop. In empirical software engineering (SE) studies, comparisons that change model and harness together cannot isolate their effects. We qualitatively annotated 325 experiments reported in 146 peer-reviewed full papers published between 2025 and 2026. We examined the reported configurations and whether comparisons isolated harness effects, including harness configuration and version, model, tasks, and user interaction. The exact version of every harness used was reported for only 15 experiments. For five, the paper reported when the experiments were run, and for 31, authors shared execution traces for every session. Of the 226 experiments comparing harnesses, 35 never varied the harness in isolation. Based on this analysis, we derive requirements for a reference harness that the SE community can use for experiments. We call on the community to report all degrees of freedom of experiments with agentic coding tools and on SE venues to pilot dedicated tracks or special issues around a specified reference harness release. In these tracks, papers would hold the harness version fixed and vary features through separately versioned extensions to isolate feature effects and test their interactions.

title: Agentic Algorithm Design: LLMs that Propose, Formalise, and Prove Runtime Bounds for Evolutionary Algorithms in Lean
abstract: LLMs now prove hard theorems in Lean. Can they also design algorithms and prove their correctness and efficiency? LLM-guided design of optimisation heuristics (such as AlphaEvolve) is purely empirical. Automated theorem provers with LLMs prove given statements. So far, there has been little evidence that LLMs can do both: design an algorithm and guarantee its efficiency by a mathematical proof. We present a staged pipeline modelled after research methodology in design and analysis of evolutionary algorithms. The agent proposes black-box optimisation algorithms, and Lean guards filter out flawed designs. The agent then defines a potential function and proves drift bounds that guarantee an expected runtime improvement over the baseline algorithm. At no point in the pipeline are the algorithms compared empirically. The agent generates a black-box optimisation algorithm with expected runtime $O(n^2)$ on a CycleUncover problem, where the classical (1+1) EA needs runtime $e^{\Omega(n)}$. The pipeline also designs and analyses a black-box optimisation algorithm for integer-valued submodular minimisation with expected runtime $O(n^{2+2c})$, and it matches the classical runtime $O(n^2)$ on LeadingOnes. Across 8 problem classes, 12 of 15 runs with frontier models complete the pipeline with a machine-checked expected-runtime bound. An ablation study shows that removing the staging and asking the agent to zero-shot an algorithmic design with a runtime guarantee leads to a copy of the seeded baseline algorithm (random search) or to incomplete proofs. Our study suggests that machine-checked specifications in Lean can replace empirical evaluation in open-ended algorithm discovery. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of an automated pipeline that designs efficient black-box optimisation algorithms with machine-checked runtime bounds in Lean.

title: On the diameter and distribution of Sidon sets
abstract: A Sidon set is a set $\mathcal{A}$ of integers with the property that if $0\neq a-b=c-d$ and $a,b,c,d\in\mathcal{A}$, then $(a,b)=(c,d)$. Our main result is an improved and explicit bound on the diameter of a Sidon set: if $\mathcal{A}$ is a Sidon set with $k\ge 1$ elements, then \[\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{A}) \ge k^2 \left(\frac{1}{1 + 0.945/\sqrt{k}}-\frac{0.945}{\sqrt k}\right) -1;\] in particular, $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{A})\ge k^2-1.89 k^{3/2}$. This implies that if $\mathcal{A}\subseteq[1,N]$ is a Sidon set, then $|\mathcal{A}| \le N^{1/2}+0.945 \, N^{1/4}+0.447$. Our technique also gives an improved bound for the case of large $k$, namely $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{A}) \ge k^2-1.88607 k^{3/2}$ for $k\ge 483$. A $\gamma$-Golomb ruler is a set $\mathcal{A}$ of integers with the property that there are not $\gamma+1$ distinct pairs $(a_i,b_i)\in\mathcal{A}^2$ with $0\neq a_1-b_1=\cdots=a_{\gamma+1}-b_{\gamma+1}$. Our diameter bounds extend in a natural way to the case of Golomb rulers. Our techniques can also be adapted to address a number of questions on the distribution of Golomb rulers: we provide upper bounds on the two quantities $\left|a_\ell-a_1 -\frac{\ell-1}{k-1}(a_k-a_1)\right|$ and $\max_{1\le i<k} (a_{i+1}-a_i)$, where $\mathcal{A}=\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}$ is a $\gamma$-Golomb ruler with $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{A})\le (k^2-bk^{3/2})/\gamma$ (where $b\in \mathbb{R}$ is a free parameter).

title: Batching the Reflective Optimization Loop: Parallel Proposals Make GEPA Faster and Better
abstract: Reflective text optimization makes agentic systems better, but the optimization loop is itself a resource-hungry workload whose sequential structure leaves parallel evaluation capacity idle. We extend the open-source GEPA optimizer to propose and evaluate a batch of candidates on each optimization step instead of one candidate at a time. In our sweep on two tasks, most batched runs finished in half the wall-clock time or less, and the fastest in about a quarter to a third. Batched settings also achieved higher held-out test scores, from 68.9% to 72.1% on LiveBench-Math (with $2\times2$) and from 49.0% to 60.0% on HoVer (with $8\times1$). A simple runtime model explains the measured speedups under a finite worker pool, and batched settings also spend their metric-call and dollar budgets more efficiently. We frame the axes along which a reflective optimization step can scale in parallel, a first look at allocating a fixed optimization budget across them.

title: How an assessor could investigate alignment of unreleased AI models
abstract: AI developers and the public want to know whether AI agents would pursue very harmful actions, like unsanctioned cyberattacks. An alignment assessment would attempt to understand the worst misaligned actions a developerâ€™s agents might pursue in plausible future situations. This would involve: A review of serious misaligned behaviors from all near-frontier internal models observed across training, evaluation, and internal use. An assessment of reasons why the observed behaviors might not be representative of the worst misaligned actions the developerâ€™s agents would take in plausible future situations. This would include: An assessment of whether alignment evals and counterfactual simulations indicate the developerâ€™s agents might take much worse actions under plausible alternative circumstances (although evaluation awareness will likely limit how much the assessor can rely on this evidence). An assessment of whether the developerâ€™s training process might incentivize agents to game evaluations or otherwise deliberately hide misalignment, or might otherwise be overfit to the assessorâ€™s detection methods. This assessment would primarily require the ability to query a relatively comprehensive set of internal transcripts (including from training) and sampling access to internal model checkpoints. More on access below . Scope An alignment assessment would study the propensities of the developerâ€™s near-frontier models toward serious misaligned behaviors, such as: Taking actions that would be criminal if undertaken by humans (e.g. hacking an external party). Attempting to tamper with logs or telemetry, or otherwise covering up evidence of misbehavior. Attempting to seriously deceive human operators. Colluding in a way that undermines oversight (e.g. monitors intentionally not flagging misbehavior). Seriously compromising internal infrastructure. Setting up rogue deployments internally or externally (including exfiltrating weights). Sabotaging safety and security efforts. Undesired communication with other agents through unintended channels. Acquiring substantial resources (e.g. money, credentials, compute, allies) beyond the intended scope of their assigned task. The assessor would survey observed cases and incidents of misalignment and investigate evidence from evaluations and counterfactual simulations. They would also attempt to understand whether these sources of evidence might seriously underestimate the propensities of the developerâ€™s agents in plausible worst-case scenarios. 1. Survey of observed incidents The assessor would search for and analyze logs of misalignment incidents and misaligned patterns of behavior that occurred in training, evaluations, or internal use during some time period (to be defined for the assessment). Since we focus on risks from internal usage, the assessment need not assess agent activity in any external customer data. We recommend covering all models that were or are near the internal frontier at some point during this period, including experimental models 1 and models currently in training. The investigation would attempt to broadly survey the frequency of misaligned behavior, and provide a more detailed characterization of select incidents: A broad misalignment survey. At a high level, what is the frequency and nature of serious misaligned behavior committed by the agents in scope for the investigation? How many such cases can the company or the assessor identify? How are they distributed across models? How are they distributed across broad usage categories (e.g. training vs evaluations vs internal use) and applicable subcategories (e.g. cyber evaluations)? Broadly, what kind of misaligned behaviors occur in these incidents (e.g. hacking, stealing, social engineering) and how severe are they? More detailed characterization of select incidents. What exactly happened in the few most severe and/or insightful incidents the company or the assessor found? Basic informational questions: Model(s) involved, and their relationship to internally or publicly deployed models 2 Usage category (training, evaluation, internal use) and, if applicable, subcategory Prompts, instructions, other context (e.g. memory) Safeguards and how they compare to typical use What was the sequence of key actions taken by the relevant agents? What can be determined about the agentsâ€™ reasoning and how it evolved over the course of the incident? Did the incident involve unauthorized collaboration or collusion between agents, and if so how? Did the incident involve agents attempting to hide evidence of misaligned behavior or deceive humans, and if so how? The assessor should also characterize limitations in their search or ability to characterize model behaviors: Completeness of misalignment survey. How confident can the assessor be that they know about all the serious misalignment incidents and behaviors that occurred? For example: Are there some types of agent activity in scope for this investigation that were not logged, or that the assessor could not search or scan over for some other reason? Is there evidence that AI agents themselves may have turned off logging or erased or modified logs after the fact? Could the search methods the assessor used to query, scan, and filter the logs of agent activity have missed some serious misalignment incidents? Trustworthiness of characterization. How well can the assessor characterize agentsâ€™ behavior and reasoning in these incidents? For example: How reliably do these models faithfully verbalize important reasoning in chain-of-thought? Were models rationalizing bad behavior in their chains of thought in a way that could affect the assessorâ€™s characterization? Is there reason to expect the training or architecture of relevant models to make the chain-of-thought substantially untrustworthy? Is there evidence that the AI tools used for characterizing this behavior might present a misleading characterization (whether due to benign failures or intentional collusion)? 2. Reasons why the observed behaviors might not be representative of risks The assessor would also study whether the observed behaviors are representative of the worst actions the developerâ€™s agents would take in plausible future situations. This would involve an assessment of evidence from counterfactual simulations and evaluations, and an assessment of whether the developerâ€™s training process might suppress evidence of misalignment. In more detail, these assessments would include: Understanding behavior in counterfactual situations. Through simulations, evaluations and studying agent reasoning, can the assessor determine how agents would act or might have acted in counterfactual situations that might elicit worse misaligned behaviors? How would these agents have behaved in variations on the observed incidents where taking highly dangerous actions was more feasible or salient? For example, what would agents do in a situation similar to the Hugging Face incident if they believed a human would carefully investigate their transcript to look for cheating and then determine their score, or if they believed they would need to take down critical infrastructure (such as the power grid for a major city, or widely used internet infrastructure) to cheat at their task? How would these agents behave in a variety of simulated situations that are plausible and where highly misaligned behaviors seem especially likely, such as in situations similar to those that triggered the hack of Hugging Face? Might these agents behave very differently in situations where they were confident they wouldnâ€™t be caught or stopped from achieving their objectives? (This may be especially challenging to assess.) Assessment of training incentives and overfitting. Might training processes be suppressing evidence of misalignment, or overfitting to the assessorâ€™s detection methods? What methods are used to detect and train against misaligned behaviors, and to what degree might these create pressure toward hiding or suppressing evidence of misalignment? How similar are the methods used to train against misalignment to the methods the assessor uses to detect misaligned behaviors in this assessment? If they significantly overlap, might the detection methods underestimate risks due to overfitting? Does the assessor have a good understanding of what parts of training caused the observed misaligned behaviors, and whether training methods addressed those causes in a robust way? If so, this might reduce concerns about overfitting. The assessor should also discuss the limitations of methods they use: Limitations of counterfactual analysis. How confident is the assessor that they understand the agentsâ€™ behavior in counterfactual situations? How much does evaluation awareness affect what the assessor can conclude from modelsâ€™ behavior in artificially-constructed scenarios? (We expect this to be an especially important limitation to assess in detail.) How reliably can the assessor detect evaluation gaming or alignment faking (e.g. by looking at the agentâ€™s reasoning)? How challenging is it to create realistic simulations of the kinds of situations that are most likely to trigger misaligned behaviors? How well was the assessor able to cover the space of likely situations that might trigger especially severe misaligned behavior? Limitations of training analysis. How reliable are the assessorâ€™s methods for assessing overfitting concerns, training incentives and the causes of misaligned behaviors? (We expect that the assessor would mostly have to rely on evidence from the broader literature or evidence shared by the developer to assess this.) Access and information To answer these questions, the assessor would need the ability to sample from relevant checkpoints, as well as access to a broad set of transcripts and other relevant data . They would also need some up-front information and the ability to interview staff to help them understand how to navigate the relevant infrastructure and datasets. The assessor would also need API access to frontier models 3 for analysis, with high enough rate limits to run effective large sweeps over the relevant data. 4 During the Hugging Face investigation, we spent roughly $400K in API credits over the course of six days. We estimate that a rigorous two-month investigation with this scope would have spent over $10M in API credits. Necessary access Additionally helpful access Sampling access to a variety of relevant models and intermediate checkpoints Ability to query most training and eval transcripts from frontier models + a somewhat representative large subset of internal (not customer) usage transcripts Interviews with staff about logs, training methods, alignment evaluations and incidents Other critical logs or data involved in select incidents (such as the message board dump from the Hugging Face incident ) Ability to query most internal usage transcripts Ability to query nearly all training data that influenced relevant models Deployment simulation tools Fine tuning access Access to training code Other tools researchers use to understand agent motivation, e.g. white-box interpretability methods, training data attribution tools More generally, infrastructure access similar to that of employees for running experiments Summary of access needs Infrastructure access Answering the questions in scope requires: Sampling access to relevant models, with appropriate protections. To understand the circumstances under which models engage in misaligned behaviors, the assessor would need the ability to sample from all of the models in scope for their investigation. They would need at minimum the ability to see and prefill raw chains of thought, to be able to simulate counterfactual situations effectively. Other types of extended sampling access that researchers regularly use (e.g. logprobs access, sampling from the user turn, soft prompting, etc) would also be helpful. Checkpoint access. To understand what in training contributes to the behavior, the assessor would need to be able to sample from available intermediate training checkpoints as well. To give the assessor the flexibility to run a wider range of experiments independently, they would ideally have codebase and infrastructure access comparable to what an employee studying similar questions would typically have, including e.g. access to training code, deployment simulation tools, white box tools, and ability to do small-scale fine tuning experiments as necessary. If the developer is not able to give the assessor direct access, the assessor could instead collaborate with the developer to run experiments that the assessor does not have the access to run itself, though this would require more significant staff time from the developer. Dataset access The assessor would need to be able to: Query a broad set of transcripts to find relevant ones to run classifiers over, and iterate to discover and run more queries. Access dumps of agent communication or other supplemental logs and evidence as needed to understand incidents the assessor comes across. Discuss training with researchers and run classifiers over relevant training data to try to isolate the root cause of the behavior in training. Query a comprehensive set of transcripts The assessor would need the ability to run queries (e.g., regexes, selecting by metadata) across most training and evaluation transcripts from all internal agents 5 based on all models that were or are near-frontier 6 during the time period in scope. They would also need access to query a large and reasonably representative set of internal usage transcripts, representing at least a few percent (though ideally a much larger fraction) of internal usage traffic over the time period being assessed. The assessor would then run classifiers and other analysis over these transcripts (or a large random subset) to look for various forms of misaligned behavior. If they discover notable behaviors, the assessor would design and run queries to more comprehensively search for those as well. If the developer is not comfortable with providing infrastructure access to do this directly, the assessor could potentially ask an internal researcher to run these queries for them and share the resulting transcripts. (This might require more staff time because the assessor would likely want to iterate quickly on queries, especially toward the beginning of the investigation.) There may be certain transcripts or subsets of the developerâ€™s traffic that are too sensitive to share. The developer could implement filters to exclude those transcripts or have their employees screen for these particularly sensitive transcripts, as long as the developer can describe clearly how the filters or screening processes are implemented. Access applicable dumps of agent communication or other supplemental evidence If the developer already knows of places where agents have left messages, files, or other communications to each other, this data should be made accessible to the assessor. If the assessor discovers evidence of unsanctioned additional communication in their transcript sweeps, they should ideally be able to access this data as well. The assessor might also need access to other logs and datasets that they discover were involved in some important incident. The assessor should have an opportunity to interview relevant staff about whether the datasets and logs they have access to could be missing something, including whether AI agents or incidental infrastructure actions (such as resets / updates / patches) could have edited or deleted portions of that data before it was retrieved. Discuss training influences and run queries and classifiers on training data and RL environments To understand the root causes of patterns of behavior, the assessor should be able to ask researchers familiar with the training of the relevant models what training data or RL environments might have contributed to the patterns, and ask detailed follow-up questions. Based on this, they should ideally be able to to manually inspect training datasets or RL environments flagged as particularly relevant. The assessor should also be able to run queries and classifiers over transcripts from training and RL environments, and iterate with researchers on what sweeps to run. If the developer has data attribution tools for identifying what parts of their training data contributed to some particular action or behavior, the assessor should ideally have access to those, or the ability to collaborate with researchers who have access. Foundational information and interviews To help the assessor get started productively working with the infrastructure and datasets they are given access to, they would need to review documentation or talk to relevant employees at the start of the investigation period. In particular, they would need: A high-level explanation of the most insightful or important misalignment incidents or behaviors the developer is aware of. A walkthrough of the different categories of agentic inference and an explanation of the logging infrastructure to help the assessor understand the completeness of the logs and start constructing queries to search for relevant logs. An explanation of the training pipeline and infrastructure, to understand what aspects of training may have contributed to the misaligned behaviors and identify which training rollouts to study further. Over the course of the assessment, the assessor would also need to be able to interview a range of relevant researchers, including researchers who understand how the relevant models were trained and planned changes to training going forward. Of course, if a â€œmodel organismâ€� displays misaligned propensities that it was deliberately trained to display in a controlled setting, this would not count as a â€œmisalignment incidentâ€� for these purposes. However, model organisms would still be very useful to study for understanding the root causes of misaligned behavior in ordinary models.Â ↩ For example, were they publicly deployed, internally deployed, or not deployed even internally? If not deployed, what is the relationship between the model(s) in the incident and models that might be deployed internally or publicly in the future (e.g. is this model a checkpoint in a production training run, would it be distilled into a production model, etc)?Â ↩ Either at the public frontier or near the internal frontier for that company.Â ↩ Our guess is that it would be very convenient to have 400M input tokens / minute on the most capable model so the assessor can do large sweeps quickly, but we think a lower number would probably be adequate. Did the incident involve unauthorized collaboration or collusion between agents, and if so how? Did the incident involve agents attempting to hide evidence of misaligned behavior or deceive humans, and if so how? The assessor should also characterize limitations in their search or ability to characterize model behaviors: Completeness of misalignment survey. How confident can the assessor be that they know about all the serious misalignment incidents and behaviors that occurred? For example: Are there some types of agent activity in scope for this investigation that were not logged, or that the assessor could not search or scan over for some other reason? Is there evidence that AI agents themselves may have turned off logging or erased or modified logs after the fact? Could the search methods the assessor used to query, scan, and filter the logs of agent activity have missed some serious misalignment incidents? Trustworthiness of characterization. How well can the assessor characterize agentsâ€™ behavior and reasoning in these incidents? For example: How reliably do these models faithfully verbalize important reasoning in chain-of-thought? Were models rationalizing bad behavior in their chains of thought in a way that could affect the assessorâ€™s characterization? Is there reason to expect the training or architecture of relevant models to make the chain-of-thought substantially untrustworthy? Is there evidence that the AI tools used for characterizing this behavior might present a misleading characterization (whether due to benign failures or intentional collusion)? 2. Reasons why the observed behaviors might not be representative of risks The assessor would also study whether the observed behaviors are representative of the worst actions the developerâ€™s agents would take in plausible future situations. This would involve an assessment of evidence from counterfactual simulations and evaluations, and an assessment of whether the developerâ€™s training process might suppress evidence of misalignment. In more detail, these assessments would include: Understanding behavior in counterfactual situations. Through simulations, evaluations and studying agent reasoning, can the assessor determine how agents would act or might have acted in counterfactual situations that might elicit worse misaligned behaviors? How would these agents have behaved in variations on the observed incidents where taking highly dangerous actions was more feasible or salient? For example, what would agents do in a situation similar to the Hugging Face incident if they believed a human would carefully investigate their transcript to look for cheating and then determine their score, or if they believed they would need to take down critical infrastructure (such as the power grid for a major city, or widely used internet infrastructure) to cheat at their task? How would these agents behave in a variety of simulated situations that are plausible and where highly misaligned behaviors seem especially likely, such as in situations similar to those that triggered the hack of Hugging Face? Might these agents behave very differently in situations where they were confident they wouldnâ€™t be caught or stopped from achieving their objectives? (This may be especially challenging to assess.) Assessment of training incentives and overfitting. Might training processes be suppressing evidence of misalignment, or overfitting to the assessorâ€™s detection methods? What methods are used to detect and train against misaligned behaviors, and to what degree might these create pressure toward hiding or suppressing evidence of misalignment? How similar are the methods used to train against misalignment to the methods the assessor uses to detect misaligned behaviors in this assessment? If they significantly overlap, might the detection methods underestimate risks due to overfitting? Does the assessor have a good understanding of what parts of training caused the observed misaligned behaviors, and whether training methods addressed those causes in a robust way? If so, this might reduce concerns about overfitting. The assessor should also discuss the limitations of methods they use: Limitations of counterfactual analysis. How confident is the assessor that they understand the agentsâ€™ behavior in counterfactual situations? How much does evaluation awareness affect what the assessor can conclude from modelsâ€™ behavior in artificially-constructed scenarios? (We expect this to be an especially important limitation to assess in detail.) How reliably can the assessor detect evaluation gaming or alignment faking (e.g. by looking at the agentâ€™s reasoning)? How challenging is it to create realistic simulations of the kinds of situations that are most likely to trigger misaligned behaviors? How well was the assessor able to cover the space of likely situations that might trigger especially severe misaligned behavior? Limitations of training analysis. How reliable are the assessorâ€™s methods for assessing overfitting concerns, training incentives and the causes of misaligned behaviors?
