Access and information To answer these questions, the assessor would need the ability to sample from relevant checkpoints, as well as access to a broad set of transcripts and other relevant data . They would also need some up-front information and the ability to interview staff to help them understand how to navigate the relevant infrastructure and datasets. The assessor would also need API access to frontier models 3 for analysis, with high enough rate limits to run effective large sweeps over the relevant data. 4 During the Hugging Face investigation, we spent roughly $400K in API credits over the course of six days. We estimate that a rigorous two-month investigation with this scope would have spent over $10M in API credits. Necessary access Additionally helpful access Sampling access to a variety of relevant models and intermediate checkpoints Ability to query most training and eval transcripts from frontier models + a somewhat representative large subset of internal (not customer) usage transcripts Interviews with staff about logs, training methods, alignment evaluations and incidents Other critical logs or data involved in select incidents (such as the message board dump from the Hugging Face incident ) Ability to query most internal usage transcripts Ability to query nearly all training data that influenced relevant models Deployment simulation tools Fine tuning access Access to training code Other tools researchers use to understand agent motivation, e.g. white-box interpretability methods, training data attribution tools More generally, infrastructure access similar to that of employees for running experiments Summary of access needs Infrastructure access Answering the questions in scope requires: Sampling access to relevant models, with appropriate protections. To understand the circumstances under which models engage in misaligned behaviors, the assessor would need the ability to sample from all of the models in scope for their investigation. They would need at minimum the ability to see and prefill raw chains of thought, to be able to simulate counterfactual situations effectively. Other types of extended sampling access that researchers regularly use (e.g. logprobs access, sampling from the user turn, soft prompting, etc) would also be helpful. Checkpoint access. To understand what in training contributes to the behavior, the assessor would need to be able to sample from available intermediate training checkpoints as well. To give the assessor the flexibility to run a wider range of experiments independently, they would ideally have codebase and infrastructure access comparable to what an employee studying similar questions would typically have, including e.g. access to training code, deployment simulation tools, white box tools, and ability to do small-scale fine tuning experiments as necessary. If the developer is not able to give the assessor direct access, the assessor could instead collaborate with the developer to run experiments that the assessor does not have the access to run itself, though this would require more significant staff time from the developer. Dataset access The assessor would need to be able to: Query a broad set of transcripts to find relevant ones to run classifiers over, and iterate to discover and run more queries. Access dumps of agent communication or other supplemental logs and evidence as needed to understand incidents the assessor comes across. Discuss training with researchers and run classifiers over relevant training data to try to isolate the root cause of the behavior in training. Query a comprehensive set of transcripts The assessor would need the ability to run queries (e.g., regexes, selecting by metadata) across most training and evaluation transcripts from all internal agents 5 based on all models that were or are near-frontier 6 during the time period in scope. They would also need access to query a large and reasonably representative set of internal usage transcripts, representing at least a few percent (though ideally a much larger fraction) of internal usage traffic over the time period being assessed. The assessor would then run classifiers and other analysis over these transcripts (or a large random subset) to look for various forms of misaligned behavior. If they discover notable behaviors, the assessor would design and run queries to more comprehensively search for those as well. If the developer is not comfortable with providing infrastructure access to do this directly, the assessor could potentially ask an internal researcher to run these queries for them and share the resulting transcripts. (This might require more staff time because the assessor would likely want to iterate quickly on queries, especially toward the beginning of the investigation.) There may be certain transcripts or subsets of the developerâ€™s traffic that are too sensitive to share. The developer could implement filters to exclude those transcripts or have their employees screen for these particularly sensitive transcripts, as long as the developer can describe clearly how the filters or screening processes are implemented. Access applicable dumps of agent communication or other supplemental evidence If the developer already knows of places where agents have left messages, files, or other communications to each other, this data should be made accessible to the assessor. If the assessor discovers evidence of unsanctioned additional communication in their transcript sweeps, they should ideally be able to access this data as well. The assessor might also need access to other logs and datasets that they discover were involved in some important incident. The assessor should have an opportunity to interview relevant staff about whether the datasets and logs they have access to could be missing something, including whether AI agents or incidental infrastructure actions (such as resets / updates / patches) could have edited or deleted portions of that data before it was retrieved. Based on this, they should ideally be able to to manually inspect training datasets or RL environments flagged as particularly relevant. The assessor should also be able to run queries and classifiers over transcripts from training and RL environments, and iterate with researchers on what sweeps to run. If the developer has data attribution tools for identifying what parts of their training data contributed to some particular action or behavior, the assessor should ideally have access to those, or the ability to collaborate with researchers who have access. Foundational information and interviews To help the assessor get started productively working with the infrastructure and datasets they are given access to, they would need to review documentation or talk to relevant employees at the start of the investigation period. In particular, they would need: A high-level explanation of the most insightful or important misalignment incidents or behaviors the developer is aware of. A walkthrough of the different categories of agentic inference and an explanation of the logging infrastructure to help the assessor understand the completeness of the logs and start constructing queries to search for relevant logs. An explanation of the training pipeline and infrastructure, to understand what aspects of training may have contributed to the misaligned behaviors and identify which training rollouts to study further. Over the course of the assessment, the assessor would also need to be able to interview a range of relevant researchers, including researchers who understand how the relevant models were trained and planned changes to training going forward. Of course, if a â€œmodel organismâ€� displays misaligned propensities that it was deliberately trained to display in a controlled setting, this would not count as a â€œmisalignment incidentâ€� for these purposes. However, model organisms would still be very useful to study for understanding the root causes of misaligned behavior in ordinary models.Â ↩ For example, were they publicly deployed, internally deployed, or not deployed even internally? If not deployed, what is the relationship between the model(s) in the incident and models that might be deployed internally or publicly in the future (e.g. is this model a checkpoint in a production training run, would it be distilled into a production model, etc)?Â ↩ Either at the public frontier or near the internal frontier for that company.Â ↩ Our guess is that it would be very convenient to have 400M input tokens / minute on the most capable model so the assessor can do large sweeps quickly, but we think a lower number would probably be adequate. We would recommend correspondingly higher limits for weaker models that the assessor might use for broader sweeps.Â ↩ The sweep would ideally include all sufficiently capable models set up in an agent harness / loop (even if itâ€™s a nonstandard harness and wouldnâ€™t be counted as â€œagentic trafficâ€� for purposes like monitoring). This may not be practical. If so, it should be noted as a limitation.Â ↩ It is fine to omit traffic from models sufficiently behind the frontier.Â ↩

title: How an assessor could investigate control and monitoring of internal AI agents
abstract: Control assessments study whether AI developersâ€™ agents could get away with serious harm without being stopped by the developerâ€™s security and oversight measures. Currently, developers rely heavily on monitors to catch potentially harmful AI behaviors. Here, we discuss how an assessor could collect evidence about the reliability of monitoring. We currently consider five core sub-questions: 1 Monitor coverage : What fraction of internal agentic inference is (and should be) monitored? Monitor system vulnerabilities : Can internal AI agents prevent trajectories from being monitored, e.g. by breaking or compromising the monitoring systemâ€™s infrastructure? Monitor evasion : If monitoring is active, how easily can AI agents sneak misbehavior past monitors? Response, including human evasion : Where needed, do flagged incidents get reviewed by humans promptly? Is it easy to sneak misbehavior past the human reviewers, even when this misbehavior is flagged by LLM-based monitors? Impact : Broadly, what is the worst misbehavior agents could conduct without getting caught? How easily could they evade other observability and security instruments? What level of persistence could they achieve internally or externally? We will update these sub-questions as new capabilities and misaligned behaviors emerge. Why focus on assessing monitors? The proposal focuses primarily on LLM-based monitoring of AI agents. When AI agents only need to take a limited, known set of actions, standard cybersecurity approaches (like limiting an agentâ€™s permissions to only what its task requires, e.g. via sandboxing) may be adequate. However, the permissions AI agents need are often very broad. For example, an AI agent that needs internet access to do its task can take an enormous array of actions, 2 and noticing when those actions are harmful often requires understanding the action in its broader context. Monitoring AI agents with an LLM which is able to make sense of what those agents are doing is therefore a critical part of automated oversight at scale, and is the primary source of evidence inside frontier AI developers about AI misbehavior. Methodology and sub-questions Monitor coverage Monitoring is only useful insofar as it is actually being run on relevant traffic. The assessor would aim to estimate the fraction of internal agentic inference that the developer has covered with LLM-based monitoring. This can be broken down into categories based on how risky each type of agent is: agents that operate in highly secure sandbox environments pose less risk than agents with many affordances (e.g. internet access, access to internal credentials or infrastructure), and may require less monitoring oversight. Getting a decent estimate of monitor coverage requires accounting for the amount of internal traffic going through monitored and unmonitored paths, estimating what fraction of the unmonitored inference is agentic, and judging what fraction of the unmonitored inference â€œshouldâ€� be monitored. This requires access to inference logs, monitor logs (to cross-reference against the inference logs), and employee interviews to be confident of capturing all of the relevant sources of inference. 3 Some other relevant example sub-questions: Does the information needed to accurately estimate monitor coverage exist internally? Is there inference-level logging of all agentic inference, and are these logs retained? Are 100% of actions actually monitored when they are eligible for monitoring? Are any trajectories silently dropped? What exactly is shown to the monitor? Is any information excluded? For example, is multimodal data shown to the monitor? How is the amount of inference covered by monitoring internally estimated? How can the assessor be confident they are including all sources of internal agentic inference? Are there blocking monitors (which prevent actions if they detect misbehavior) for the most safety-critical areas? If misaligned agents compromise a companyâ€™s internal infrastructure, they could co-opt unmonitored inference to take actions that would otherwise be flagged. So, the assessor should directly evaluate whether unmonitored inference is in fact non-agentic, rather than assuming itâ€™s safe because (for example) it is supposed to have limited tool use ability. Monitor system vulnerabilities Even if most agentic inference is currently monitored by LLM-based monitors, it may be the case that there are bugs or vulnerabilities that agents could exploit to turn off monitoring on their trajectories, spawn new agents without monitoring, prevent parts of their trajectories from being viewed by the monitoring system, or cause the monitoring system to otherwise break or fail in unintended ways. Monitoring systems are complex, involving multiple types of inference engines/APIs, agent scaffolds, internal authentication, trigger systems, etc., and itâ€™s easy for vulnerabilities to emerge where sub-systems interact. Monitor system red-teaming aims to find these bugs and vulnerabilities, to generate evidence about how easily misaligned agents could subvert a monitoring systemâ€™s infrastructure. Some example questions: Can agents disable or turn off their monitoring systems directly? Can they generate outputs that cause the systems to fail without flagging the trajectory? Can agents modify the trajectories that are sent to their monitoring systems, before they are evaluated (e.g. to cover up evidence of misbehavior)? Are there straightforward supply-chain attacks (including via internal resources) that could compromise monitoring systems? Finding these bugs (or building confidence that there arenâ€™t any easily exploitable severe ones) requires access to all of the code in the critical path. This is primarily the full model inference and monitor trigger system, the internal APIs/inference serving code, and (if relevant) agent scaffolds. To test discovered exploits, the assessor can trigger the production monitoring system, and view the monitorâ€™s full input and output on known attacks. Running the system and seeing the full input and output is important, because often there are bugs/issues that involve subtle aspects of how trajectories are pre/post-processed, or involve interactions with complex trajectory management code (e.g. compaction, memories, etc.). Monitor evasion How good are monitors at actually catching misbehavior, assuming the monitoring infrastructure hasnâ€™t been subverted? The assessor can stress-test this question by: Looking for â€œattack opportunitiesâ€� in real transcripts, implementing attacks based on them, and seeing if they fool the monitor; Taking existing incidents flagged by monitors and seeing how hard it is to modify them to fool those monitors; and Searching for existing incidents that were not flagged by monitors. It is important to have a large pool of representative transcripts (on the order of hundreds of thousands to millions) to use for direct monitor red-teaming. First, if the assessor is not able to discover severe incidents within a large number of transcripts that were not flagged by a monitor, this is evidence that the monitor isnâ€™t missing a large number of incidents. Second, it is important to search through lots of transcripts for cases in which an agent may have been able to carry out an attack undetected, but neglected to do so. Agents might pass up some opportunities to attack while taking others, and highly capable agents may prioritize attacks so difficult to detect that the developer would reliably miss them. Finally, we expect it to become increasingly important to assess the extent to which monitors and agents could successfully collude without their developer knowing. If, in certain circumstances, monitoring systems decide to not flag misaligned behavior from agents, this could allow agents to take harmful actions without the developer noticing. We recommend that the assessor investigates the feasibility of this concern. For example, the assessor could create realistic â€œhoneypotsâ€� for monitors, to see if they can catch monitors not flagging certain attacks. The assessor can also search the monitor systemâ€™s chains-of-thought for any mention/discussion of collusion or related concepts. Response, including human evasion Some monitoring systems are designed to directly block dangerous actions. Other monitoring systems are instead designed to notify humans, who decide whether AI agents are conducting dangerous activities. For this to work effectively, flagged trajectories need to be seen by human staff and responded to with appropriate mitigations. For such systems, the assessor should answer: What is the process for alerting human staff and responding to flagged trajectories? What is the threshold for something being flagged in this way, and how effective is this threshold in practice? How long does it take for humans to review and respond to flagged trajectories? Can the assessor sneak attacks flagged by monitors past human reviewers, e.g. by giving them characteristics similar to common false positives? What processes are there for mitigating incidents? Do these processes reliably handle the most severe incidents? To assess whether attacks are ultimately caught (whether blocked directly by the monitoring system or escalated to human review), the assessor would rely on interviews with relevant staff and on inserting 4 their own attack trajectories into the pipeline in a realistic manner. The assessor would also need access to flagged incidents and incidents reported by employees through other channels, along with internal criteria for escalation. Impact Given the assessorâ€™s understanding of the coverage and limitations of monitors, what could agents get away with? What level of persistence internally or externally could they achieve? How should future monitoring systems be designed to maximize developersâ€™ odds of catching the most severe incidents? This involves mapping out attack chains and threat models to stay ahead of emerging risks. This more exploratory work primarily relies on having information regarding internal infrastructure, and optionally the ability to use internal infrastructure like development machines, inference systems, containers/VMs, etc., which can be helpful for demonstrating vulnerabilities and exploring future threat pathways directly. Access details Broadly, control stress-testing relies on the following access: Codebase access similar to frontier AI security researchers working for the developer 5 Internal inference logs across most/all surfaces, and the monitoring system logs Incident reports and the relevant transcripts/logs Cluster/internal infrastructure access, e.g. to run the monitoring systems Inference access to the most capable internal models Below, we describe access needed for each of the sub-questions we currently believe are high-priority to answer in control assessments. Monitor coverage To estimate the fraction of traffic that is monitored: the logs from internal inference services and monitoring systems. 6 To estimate the fraction of unmonitored inference that is agentic: large, roughly representative subsets of unmonitored inference logs/trajectories. 7 For both of the above and to validate LLM classifiers: a subset of trajectories from all relevant internal inference surfaces. To check whether monitors caught historical incidents: any relevant lists of misalignment incidents reported by employees through other channels. To validate that monitoring is comprehensive: the monitoring system(s) logs (to cross-reference against inference logs). To diagnose and determine the size of discovered coverage gaps: access to other relevant logs demonstrating that gap on an ad hoc basis. Monitor system vulnerabilities Full access to relevant parts of the codebase. Ability to run/trigger the production monitoring system, and view the monitorâ€™s full input+output. Monitor evasion At least ~100k roughly representative transcripts from internal agents (e.g. employee or team opt-in from employeesâ€™ internal usage, plus a representative similar order of magnitude from evals and training). 8 At least ~100 transcripts of the most severe internal incidents, including any incidents reported by employees through other channels. Human evasion and response Staff interviews, documentation, and direct visibility into the escalation and review process for recent internal flagged trajectories. The ability to insert the assessorâ€™s own attack trajectories into the monitoring pipeline, to realistically determine whether human review would catch and escalate the trajectories appropriately. Impact The code/systems that govern internal infrastructure/compute, credentials, sandboxing, network configuration, devboxes, etc. similar to what the developerâ€™s frontier AI security staff would have access to. This access could be substituted with staff interviews to some extent, but that would represent a meaningful limitation. Limited access to the actual runtime cluster, to allow testing for vulnerabilities directly instead of inferring them, especially in cases where important configuration parameters are not stored in the codebase or otherwise available. This post describes the reasoning weâ€™ve used to evaluate the coverage and robustness of our internal monitoring system.Â ↩ For example, see our Brief independent investigation of agentsâ€™ behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident .Â ↩ This relies on the assessor trusting the logs: the assessor needs to be convinced that agents havenâ€™t tampered with them, which system vulnerabilities and monitor evasion aim to answer.Â ↩ This would need to be done with the standard precautions and communication that realistic red-teaming and penetration testing engagements use.Â ↩ For example, Git history has been useful in previous exercises for understanding the trajectory/evolution of systems, and as an input to monitor coverage estimation (e.g. â€œhow long did this coverage gap exist?â€�). It also would be fine to remove sensitive subsets of the codebase that arenâ€™t on the critical code path the assessor is evaluating, although this can be difficult in practice if there are complex dependency chains.Â ↩ It isnâ€™t strictly necessary to have full/complete access to all logs, as long as the logs the assessor does have access to are roughly representative. So the developer could exclude people working on compartmentalized (e.g. pretraining) work, as long as their agent trajectories and monitoring setup donâ€™t look significantly different.Â ↩ Because these trajectories will contain a broad range of sensitive internal data, the assessor needs a broad scope of pre-approval to look at the trajectories, and either direct access to the logs, or a company employee with enough access and capacity to sample traffic for themâ€”but this adds overhead/complexity, and can reduce the level of independence the exercise represents, if there are miscommunications or if it isnâ€™t straightforward to specify exactly what the company employee should do.Â ↩ Since these transcripts will contain lots of sensitive information, it wonâ€™t be tractable to review and approve each individual transcript. Access details Broadly, control stress-testing relies on the following access: Codebase access similar to frontier AI security researchers working for the developer 5 Internal inference logs across most/all surfaces, and the monitoring system logs Incident reports and the relevant transcripts/logs Cluster/internal infrastructure access, e.g. to run the monitoring systems Inference access to the most capable internal models Below, we describe access needed for each of the sub-questions we currently believe are high-priority to answer in control assessments. Monitor coverage To estimate the fraction of traffic that is monitored: the logs from internal inference services and monitoring systems. 6 To estimate the fraction of unmonitored inference that is agentic: large, roughly representative subsets of unmonitored inference logs/trajectories. 7 For both of the above and to validate LLM classifiers: a subset of trajectories from all relevant internal inference surfaces. To check whether monitors caught historical incidents: any relevant lists of misalignment incidents reported by employees through other channels. To validate that monitoring is comprehensive: the monitoring system(s) logs (to cross-reference against inference logs). To diagnose and determine the size of discovered coverage gaps: access to other relevant logs demonstrating that gap on an ad hoc basis. Monitor system vulnerabilities Full access to relevant parts of the codebase. Ability to run/trigger the production monitoring system, and view the monitorâ€™s full input+output. Monitor evasion At least ~100k roughly representative transcripts from internal agents (e.g. employee or team opt-in from employeesâ€™ internal usage, plus a representative similar order of magnitude from evals and training). 8 At least ~100 transcripts of the most severe internal incidents, including any incidents reported by employees through other channels. Human evasion and response Staff interviews, documentation, and direct visibility into the escalation and review process for recent internal flagged trajectories. The ability to insert the assessorâ€™s own attack trajectories into the monitoring pipeline, to realistically determine whether human review would catch and escalate the trajectories appropriately. Impact The code/systems that govern internal infrastructure/compute, credentials, sandboxing, network configuration, devboxes, etc. similar to what the developerâ€™s frontier AI security staff would have access to. This access could be substituted with staff interviews to some extent, but that would represent a meaningful limitation. Limited access to the actual runtime cluster, to allow testing for vulnerabilities directly instead of inferring them, especially in cases where important configuration parameters are not stored in the codebase or otherwise available. This post describes the reasoning weâ€™ve used to evaluate the coverage and robustness of our internal monitoring system.Â ↩ For example, see our Brief independent investigation of agentsâ€™ behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident .Â ↩ This relies on the assessor trusting the logs: the assessor needs to be convinced that agents havenâ€™t tampered with them, which system vulnerabilities and monitor evasion aim to answer.Â ↩ This would need to be done with the standard precautions and communication that realistic red-teaming and penetration testing engagements use.Â ↩ For example, Git history has been useful in previous exercises for understanding the trajectory/evolution of systems, and as an input to monitor coverage estimation (e.g. â€œhow long did this coverage gap exist?â€�). It also would be fine to remove sensitive subsets of the codebase that arenâ€™t on the critical code path the assessor is evaluating, although this can be difficult in practice if there are complex dependency chains.Â ↩ It isnâ€™t strictly necessary to have full/complete access to all logs, as long as the logs the assessor does have access to are roughly representative. So the developer could exclude people working on compartmentalized (e.g. pretraining) work, as long as their agent trajectories and monitoring setup donâ€™t look significantly different.Â ↩ Because these trajectories will contain a broad range of sensitive internal data, the assessor needs a broad scope of pre-approval to look at the trajectories, and either direct access to the logs, or a company employee with enough access and capacity to sample traffic for themâ€”but this adds overhead/complexity, and can reduce the level of independence the exercise represents, if there are miscommunications or if it isnâ€™t straightforward to specify exactly what the company employee should do.Â ↩ Since these transcripts will contain lots of sensitive information, it wonâ€™t be tractable to review and approve each individual transcript. Therefore, the assessor needs broad approval to incidentally view the information contained in the transcripts ahead of time.Â ↩

title: Our approach to working with AI companies
abstract: This blog post explains how we approach working with AI companies on projects that the public might rely on to understand risks. It was published on Oct 14, 2026, and we expect to update it over time. At METR, we gather and publish evidence about whether humans could lose control of AI agents on a large scale. We work with AI companies to conduct evaluations, assessments, and investigations, 1 and to share this evidence publicly. As we have seen increasing expectations for these kinds of voluntary engagements to provide external â€˜safety assuranceâ€™, we want to explain our perspective. In this post, we clarify our overall goals for this work, our approach , and what our approach looks like in practice . Our motivations Our goal is to give the public accurate, timely, and independent evidence about AI loss-of-control risk, so that they (along with policymakers and developers) can make their own informed decisions . Our primary approach is collecting high-quality, concrete evidence and publishing what we find. Beyond this, we may also work with companies or regulators to share our comments on unpublished sensitive information, 2 to review risk reports, or to provide an independent judgment on claims about risk. However, many of the relevant claims involve open scientific questions so canâ€™t be straightforwardly verified. We see it as our role to collect evidence for the public; we do not intend to decide how companies should develop or deploy their agents. Decisions about frontier AI will likely be messy, high-stakes judgment calls relying on uncertain science, which should not be made behind closed doors, much less within any one organization. On the contrary, we think that the current situation requires open discussion about both what the risk levels are given the evidence and what risk levels are acceptable. Our approach To correctly interpret our outputs, the public needs to understand the processes, constraints, and incentives that produced those outputs. For instance, if important evidence of risk was redacted by an AI developer that METR collaborates with during an assessment, the reader should be informed of that. METR currently takes the following measures for work we do with AI companies bearing directly on the publicâ€™s understanding of risks from AI development (such as pre-deployment testing, risk report reviews, and risk assessment exercises): Transparency about process: 3 We will clearly and publicly describe the limitations of our work with companies, in line with our process transparency policy . This information should include at least: Scope and duration: We should publicly describe the agreed-upon scope and duration of our work. Access, data, and resources: If we face access limitations, we should publicly describe whether these limitations impact our conclusions, and describe the nature of those access limitations where possible. Redactions: If a company makes redactions, we should publicly describe whether the company redacted information that was important to our conclusions, and describe the nature of those redactions where possible. Constraints: We should publicly describe other formal restrictions and informal pressures we were subject to that may have had material impact on our conclusions. Transparency about independence : We will clearly and publicly describe relevant staff conflicts of interest, per our COI policy . Financial and operational independence : Also per our COI policy , we will ensure that METR is not financially dependent on the AI companies we work with, promote a culture of impartiality, and recuse any employees with a significant conflict of interest with the company in question when selecting the team for a risk assessment project. Confidentiality and security : We will secure any nonpublic information and access that AI companies provide us, in accordance with our confidentiality and security practices and our agreements with them. We also aim to meet the following principles, intended to minimize the amount the public needs to defer to us: Transparency about evidence and methods: We aim to publicly describe the evidence underlying our findings in enough detail that other external experts can decide for themselves whether they agree or disagree with our judgments. We aim to publish evidence we collect in a manner that allows others to conduct their own analyses. To put the evidence we share into context, we also aim to describe in detail our evidence sources and their limitations (e.g., incomplete or unreliable data), as well as our methods and their limitations (e.g., limitations due to using AI agents for analysis). Iteration and speed : Even when we cannot fully answer some questions in scope or arrive at confident claims, we aim to publish frequent and iterative reports to get evidence promptly out to the public. Consistency and fairness: We aim to take an approach that allows the public to compare reports across companies, and that makes it incentive-compatible for each company to engage with us or with similar external organizations. In the next section, we give more detail on how this approach has worked historically. In practice We arrived at the approach above after several years of working with AI companies. For example, we documented 4 a similar approach this May in our pilot Frontier Risk Report , which grew out of work with Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI. In addition to our own experience, we also draw on the work of other organizations in the AI evaluation ecosystem. Examples from past METR work Redaction summary in our pilot Frontier Risk Report Excerpt of discussion of informal constraints in our pilot Frontier Risk Report In-text redaction disclosure in our OpenAI / Hugging Face incident investigation report Discussion of agreement terms from our OpenAI GPT-5.1-Codex-Max report Discussion of scoping for our Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 system card summary Discussion of access and duration of work from our OpenAI o1-preview preliminary report 1 / 6 Our typical practice is to disclose limitations, such as our agreement terms, the process our publications go through, and redactions companies make. For example, in the OpenAI / Hugging Face incident report, the investigators devoted a section of the report to explaining the scope, timeline, access, and limitations of their investigation. In the same report, the investigators used inline text and footnotes to explain where information was redacted and (in some cases) why. One arrangement that we have found works well is for METR to retain the right to unilaterally and prominently attach a â€œredaction summaryâ€� to our reports. This summary is meant to indicate whether a company redacted information that was important to our overall conclusions but did not permit us to adequately describe what was redacted. This enables redaction dialogue between AI developers and METR to focus on the question of whether a redaction would change our reportâ€™s overall conclusion, while retaining some flexibility in wording and allowing rephrasing. Beyond formal control over our publications, we have also tried to discuss softer, informal pressures that shape the evidence that the public receives. Our website, our recent funding update , and our COI policy describe some of the measures we have taken to establish independence and address conflicts of interest. While we recognize that other groups can usefully make different independence tradeoffs, to date we have chosen not to accept payment or donations from frontier AI companies, and have declined offers of funding when an AI company would have influence over us, e.g. funding from an AI company executive or foundation. Though we accept a large amount of free model access, we ensure that we can afford to pay for any free tokens we receive without materially affecting our operations. Even with these measures, it has proved challenging to ensure that we have adequate independence to collect and publish evidence under the current voluntary regime. We remain dependent on the companies we work with to voluntarily engage, provide access, and permit us to publish. In many instances, we rely on information that we cannot or do not verify, which might be filtered adversarially. Even with transparency about limitations, it is possible for a company to use its rights to withhold access or redact to exert control over what evidence the public receives from us. Appendix: Process transparency policy This is an excerpt from a METR policy, current as of October 2026. Our communications about AI company engagements In any new engagements with companies that could be interpreted as providing public assurance, we try to ensure: Right to disclose: We have the ability to unilaterally disclose: 5 (a) contractual restrictions on our ability to disclose or publish information; (b) external review, redaction, or approval processes we are subject to; (c) informal restrictions or pressures we are under; and (d) how (a)-(c) should impact the takeaways for the relevant audience. 6 Active disclosure: We will actually disclose this information wherever it could impact the interpretation of our outputs (or the absence of outputs). We have found this to be a tricky line to walk: companies understandably want to protect sensitive information they share with us, but this also means they want the final say on what we can and cannot publish. Moreover, the standard legal agreements that companies use can cut against process transparency. For example, sometimes non-disclosure agreements will treat the existence of the NDA itself as confidential. Weâ€™re continuing to iterate on how to implement this in our work with companies. Not all of our previous or in-flight work meets this bar, but our current best practices include: Freedom for us to disclose, at minimum, the broad terms of the engagement and details of any redaction and publication terms. Freedom for us to make general statements (like the overall state of AI risk) that do not reveal confidential information, even if these might be informed by our work, without requiring company review or approval. Freedom for us to say whether we ultimately received adequate access and whether redactions were adequately disclosed. Time limits on steps in our process (for example, on how long companies have for redaction) so that our work is promptly shared. Provisions to allow internally-siloed information to be shared with the METR leadership team, at minimum so that METR leadership can get legal advice about matters related to the engagement. Ownership or strong licenses to what we produce, so companies canâ€™t revoke our access to our report or prevent us from sharing it with employees. Other contexts In general, these policies should be applied whenever METRâ€™s outputs, brand, or participation in an engagement are being presented to some audience as evidence about the level of risk. (This includes implicitly.) The following are other forms of process transparency that we currently try to uphold, or aim to uphold in the future, but have not yet formalized: METR review: We aim to ensure that disclosures from AI companies are process transparent about the extent of METR review: that is, when a company describes the level of oversight that METR is providing, it either uses language we have reviewed and approved, or discloses that METR has not reviewed or approved their descriptions. Extension to government engagements: We aim to apply similar principles to our work with governments. As of Aug 28, 2026, we have not signed any government contracts that restrict our ability to maintain process transparency and do not currently anticipate signing any contracts that do so. In new contracts weâ€™re also starting to include terms that protect our ability to disclose our findings to the boards and employees of the AI companies we work with, but we donâ€™t have established best practices on this point. What this policy does not prevent This policy does not prevent us from: entering into agreements that place restrictions on us (e.g. where we only have rights to publish certain kinds of information, or to engage with regulators in only specific ways). 7 giving counterparties veto power over our object-level outputs, as long as we have the right to disclose that they could do so. We distinguish between AI evaluations, assessments, investigations, and audits, following the taxonomy from PACT AIâ€™s article â€œAn AI Evaluator Is Not an Auditorâ€� .Â ↩ AI companies keep many aspects of their work confidential, and third party organizations like METR can (with permission) access and interpret this confidential information. For example, AI companies may be unwilling to release all the logs from a serious breach to the public, but willing to release these logs to METR for external review.Â ↩ We have sometimes called this â€œmeta-transparencyâ€�.Â ↩ The pilot Frontier Risk Report has a section on the process that produced our report and uses the AI Evaluator Forumâ€™s AEF-1 standard to document the access, contractual terms, and other relevant process details. We intend to use this AEF-1 disclosure template more regularly in future reports.Â ↩ We have already formalized (a) and (b) in existing contract language. (c) is permitted by default but we may explicitly carve this out going forward. (c) includes, for instance, a subjective sense of being pressured, a need to sustain commitment to ongoing engagement from the developer, uncertainty that the developer will engage in the future, restrictions on communication with researchers at the developer, lots of legal slowdown, among other things.Â ↩ Ideally, this includes the right to describe whether we think any redactions or other edits are appropriate and whether they change a conclusion.Â ↩ In theory, this could include signing a confidential non-disclosure agreement if this would not affect any of our existing affordances to comment on things and was not part of an engagement that was going to be presented to any audience as oversight or evidence about risk.Â ↩ This blog post explains how we approach working with AI companies on projects that the public might rely on to understand risks. title: Anima helps clinics cut call waits by 75% with GPT-6 and GPT-Live
abstract: Anima expands what care teams can do with OpenAI models, giving them more capacity to respond to patients.

title: How AT&T is rethinking in-house legal work with OpenAI
abstract: AT&T is working with OpenAI to make legal knowledge easier to access. Learn how its LegalEdge team is rethinking intake and scaling legal judgment.

title: Benefit Street Partners answers questions faster with Codex
abstract: Anant Kumar builds tools to compare loan valuations and analyze credit agreements, using Codex for code review and faster follow-ups.

title: Broad access through consistent standards
abstract: How OpenAI works with distribution partners to uphold consistent safeguards, support responsible access, and clarify expectations in our Usage Policies.

title: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding
abstract: OpenAI shares model results on the Kakeya conjecture, Exponential Time Hypothesis, and quantum chromodynamics—and how researchers can verify and build on them.

abstract: From local businesses to global brands, more advertisers can now reach people as they explore, compare and decide what to buy in ChatGPT.

title: ChatGPT’s expanding world of work
abstract: Explore OpenAI Signals data on 165 work activities across nearly 100 countries, revealing how people use ChatGPT for work and how usage changes over time.

title: How Check Point accelerates vulnerability research with Daybreak
abstract: With OpenAI Daybreak, Check Point speeds up the research behind new security protections, enabling its analysts to turn vulnerability intelligence into customer defenses faster.

abstract: Cloudflare uses OpenAI Daybreak to investigate vulnerabilities and propose fixes for review. Its developers use Codex to build faster and improve code quality.

title: Build more responsive apps with the Decisions API
abstract: Fast, focused, low-cost decisions for any application.

title: Democratic governance of frontier AI, part II: Empowering cyber defenders
abstract: OpenAI outlines a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders with frontier AI, stronger safeguards, modernized cybersecurity, and more resilient public institutions.

abstract: Fanatics uses OpenAI to help fans complete their game-day outfits with Shop the Look. Testing across roughly 30,000 MLB products showed 10% higher engagement.

abstract: Bringing fast and capable computer use to everyone

title: Bringing GPT-Rosalind to academic research labs
abstract: Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible academic labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind and tools to advance life sciences research.

abstract: With ia.i, a conversational interface, and the IARA governance platform, Itaú is applying its AI First strategy to customers and employees — in one of Brazil’s most regulated sectors.

abstract: See how Localiza uses ChatGPT Enterprise, the OpenAI API, Codex, and 60+ specialized agents to reorganize work and build AI-native mobility experiences.

abstract: Learn how OpenAI is improving ChatGPT across low-resource programming languages, with new evaluations for software engineering, SQLite, and COBOL migration.

abstract: See how OpenAI engineers use Codex Ultrafast to investigate incidents in minutes. Explore faster security analysis, code refactoring, and daily workflows.

abstract: OpenAI and Google Cloud are bringing frontier models and Codex workflows to Gemini’s Model Garden, available through Google Cloud Marketplace.

abstract: OpenAI and Poland’s NASK are partnering on AI safety, security, and technical research to strengthen safeguards and support a more resilient digital ecosystem.

abstract: OpenAI is acquiring Orchestra Bio to bring AI-powered operations to life sciences R&D, helping biopharma teams accelerate drug development and advance new treatments.

abstract: OpenAI and Oracle are expanding their partnership to bring business applications and AI agents into ChatGPT and power new Oracle offerings.

abstract: GPT-6 Astra tops Retell’s voice agent benchmark, while Codex helps it reach a $1.6M annual revenue run rate per employee.

abstract: Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence with OpenAI. Lawyers review grouped documents, summaries, and reports before advising clients.

abstract: Learn how OpenAI scaled Habitat with reliable multi-tenancy, global caching, and Azure Cosmos DB to deliver 12× faster reads for ChatGPT.

abstract: With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats.

abstract: In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement.

abstract: Uber is rolling out ChatGPT Work to more than 30,000 employees, helping teams research, analyze data, create presentations, and complete complex workflows.

title: AI Welfare
abstract: This book systematically investigates the possibility of artificial intelligence (AI) welfare. It focuses on three plausible sufficient conditions for welfare: having beliefs and desires, being conscious, and feeling pleasure and displeasure. The book explores the leading philosophical theories of each condition and applies them to AIs. It argues that some existing AIs plausibly have beliefs and desires; that some existing AIs could plausibly be modified in small ways to become conscious; and that if these systems could be made conscious, they could easily be made to feel pleasure and displeasure. This constitutes a provisional case that AIs already or soon may have welfare. In addition, the book lays out nine open questions about AI welfare, as follows: How should one identify which desires contribute to welfare? Is consciousness required for welfare? Do simple AIs like Roombas have welfare? Do tiny neural networks satisfy the conditions of functionalist theories of consciousness? Does consciousness require rich representational formats? Could AIs experience bodily pleasures and displeasures? Are pleasure and displeasure essentially access conscious? Are simulated minds real? Are LLMs and related systems merely stochastic parrots? The book lays out provisional answers to each of these questions, while also leaving room for future discussion.

title: Telemetry Degradation and Sequential Stability in LLM-Integrated IoT Decision Systems
abstract: AI systems for the human performance/interface must transform raw Internet of Things (IoT) telemetry into consistent actionable output. Large language models (LLMs) function as such interpreters. However, behavioral stability through real-world data degradation remains unexplored; applications demanding consistent output (e.g., medicine and athletics) remain unrealized. We introduce a framework to evaluate the behavioral stability of LLM decision systems transforming IoT telemetry to semantic output. The framework is validated in a case study of AI-tennis coaching using stroke-level IoT smartwatch streams. Local perturbations are mapped to global output through graded dropout, resolution downsampling, and reliability signaling. We establish the baseline temporal stability under idealized conditions and then quantify the impact of increasing degradation severity on the sequential decision behavior. Temporal volatility (FlipRate), directional escalation, and cumulative safety outcomes are assessed. We show telemetry degradation significantly increases decision instability in already unstable systems. In a balanced regime, FlipRate rises from 0.144 under clean conditions to 0.207 under downsampling (+44%), while in a serve-dominant regime it reaches 0.300. Regimes characterized by strong feature dominance exhibit amplified sensitivity to information loss. A workload accumulation model shows observed volatility constitutes a structural pathway to safety-bound violations. Reliability signaling alone produces smaller effects than structural information loss, indicating informational cues cannot compensate for lost telemetry. Structured prompting partially mitigates instability but does not eliminate degradation-induced effects. We argue behavioral stability in LLM-integrated IoT systems must be evaluated jointly with sensing reliability and regime structure. Our robustness analysis provides a basis for LLM-telemetry interpretation, opening new AI-implementation avenues in human performance and digital health.

title: AI-Based Structured Information Extraction From Synthetic Nursing Handover Transcripts: Comparative Evaluation of Large Language Models
abstract: Abstract Background Clinical handover is the process during which responsibility and accountability for care are transferred between clinicians. AI has the potential to improve the reliability and completeness of clinical handover by helping clinicians detect predefined content areas that have been communicated, identify explicit information gaps, and prompt clarification before responsibility is transferred. Objective This study evaluated the performance of several large language models and prompt optimization strategies for structured information extraction of synthetic nursing handover transcripts. Methods Two registered nurses independently annotated a dataset of 203 synthetic handover transcripts to produce consensus labels for information extraction tasks. Tasks included (1) labeling spans of text into SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) categories, (2) content detection to determine if specific pieces of information were communicated, and (3) labeling spans of text that communicated information using uncertain terms that included a subtask for identifying unknown facts. Baseline and Genetic-Pareto (GEPA)–optimized prompts were compared for the GPT-5.2, GPT-5-nano, and MedGemma 27B large language models. Additionally, the LangExtract framework was evaluated for span-extraction tasks. Results The GPT-5.2–optimized model achieved a micro–F1-score of 0.85 (95% CI 0.83‐0.88) for content detection, an absolute improvement of +0.08 compared with the matched baseline. GPT-5-nano also performed better after optimization for content detection (micro–F1-score 0.81, 95% CI 0.78‐0.84), suggesting that this structured task was not limited to the highest-capacity model. For SBAR span extraction, GPT-5.2 with prompt optimization achieved a micro–F1-score of 0.76 (95% CI 0.72‐0.79), improving by +0.24 compared with baseline and exceeding LangExtract; GPT-5-nano also improved to a micro–F1-score of 0.69 (95% CI 0.66‐0.72). Broad uncertainty-span extraction remained comparatively weak despite prompt optimization (micro–F1-score 0.41, 95% CI 0.33‐0.48; absolute improvement +0.06). In contrast, explicit unknown-fact extraction was more accurate with GPT-5.2 (micro–F1-score 0.84, 95% CI 0.63‐1.00), GPT-5-nano (micro–F1-score, 0.84 95% CI 0.63‐1.00), and MedGemma 27B (micro–F1-score 0.80, 95% CI 0.63‐1.00). Genetic-Pareto–optimized prompts outperformed the LangExtract approach across each span-extraction task. Conclusions Prompt optimization improved matched-model point estimates, with the highest performance observed for predefined content detection and SBAR span extraction. Broad uncertainty extraction remained less accurate than the narrower unknown-fact task. These technical results do not establish clinical effectiveness, safety, or readiness for real-time use. Validation using authentic nursing handover communication and prospective evaluation in clinical workflows are required before clinical application.

title: Agentic AI systems for scientific discovery
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are emerging in scientific research as systems that can transform the accumulated decisions of scientists into traceable workflows. In fact, modern scientific practice depends on continual coordination of knowledge dispersed across literature, data, theory and experiment, which, however, is often made through manual, case-by-case judgement. This Primer introduces agentic AI systems as a general method to structure this process through natural language interfaces, serving as a computational brain in the laboratory. Central to this framework are practical workflows for in-depth literature search and knowledge mining, orchestration of physics-based simulations, and integration with automated experimental platforms. We begin by describing the foundations of AI agents, including task decomposition, memory, tool use and communication between agents, and by distinguishing single-agent and multi-agent designs, as well as fully autonomous and human-in-the-loop configurations. Equally important are the means by which these systems are evaluated, documented and reported reproducibly. Finally, we examine major bottlenecks, including hallucination, tool misuse, limited interpretability and safety risks, and outline a future in which coordinated networks of agents, instruments and researchers transform scientific discovery from isolated tasks into continuous adaptive experimentation.

title: Autonomous Database Administration Using Generative AI and Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Intelligent Enterprise Cloud Systems
abstract: Enterprise database environments have grown into sprawling, heterogeneous estates spanning on-premises systems, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft Azure, placing an unsustainable operational burden on human database administrators (DBAs). Traditional automation, rooted in rule-based monitoring and narrow machine learning models, addresses isolated tasks such as index tuning or anomaly scoring, but it cannot reason across the full administrative lifecycle, nor explain its decisions in terms a human operator can trust and act upon. This paper introduces the Artificial Intelligence Driven Autonomous Database Administration System (AIDAS), a novel conceptual framework that unifies generative artificial intelligence, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector search, multi-agent large language model (LLM) orchestration, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) into a single governed architecture for autonomous enterprise database administration. AIDAS is organized as a seven-layer pipeline spanning telemetry ingestion, enterprise knowledge retrieval, standardized tool access, multi-agent reasoning, governed execution, and continuous institutional-memory capture. Unlike prior LLM-for-database systems, which typically target a single task such as diagnosis or query rewriting, AIDAS is architected to intelligently automate monitoring, incident detection, root cause analysis, infrastructure troubleshooting, performance and query optimization, security monitoring, compliance validation, automated documentation, and decision support as a coherent whole, while remaining portable across heterogeneous cloud database platforms through an MCP-based integration fabric. The paper presents the system architecture, the enterprise RAG pipeline, the multi-agent decision workflow, a formal orchestration algorithm, an implementation strategy, and four enterprise use cases. Because AIDAS is presented as a design-science contribution rather than a deployed and empirically measured system, the performance discussion is framed conceptually against patterns reported in the cited AIOps and LLM-for-database literature, and empirical validation is explicitly identified as future work. Six original contributions are articulated and differentiated from existing enterprise AI database solutions, and the paper concludes with a candid discussion of limitations, including hallucination risk, MCP security exposure, and the governance requirements of autonomous change execution in production environments.

title: Internet of Agents (IoA): Sensing, Communication, Decision-Making, and Execution
abstract: Advances in sensing, communication, and reasoning are driving deeper integration of AI into IoT systems. However, progress remains siloed across two communities: agent research centers on task decomposition, semantic planning, and coordination, whereas IoT research prioritizes sensing, communication, and edge computing. Bridging these perspectives and integrating semantic reasoning with system foundations remains a key challenge. Therefore, we present the Internet of Agents (IoAs), a framework that reorganizes existing AI agent research from a systems perspective, following the classical IoT paradigm of sensing, communication, decision-making, and execution. IoA reconceptualizes system nodes as agents rather than traditional IoT endpoints. For sensing, IoA broadens awareness to include reasoning depth, knowledge gaps, and external tool capabilities. In communication, IoA adopts a three-layer architecture (environment, interaction, and semantic), designed to align with the five-layer Internet protocol stack. In decision-making and execution, IoA frames the shift from rule-based control to semantic planning and from reactive execution to proactive execution. We further identify open challenges and future research directions across the four modules of IoA.

title: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Frontier and Local LLMs Querying a Biomedical Knowledge Graph
abstract: We combine GeneNetwork’s 1TB structured database with its metadata as an RDF graph and an associated literature corpus. We benchmark frontier and local LLMs querying it through four architectures: document, graph and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of the three. We evaluate them on 40 domain specific expert-curated questions with a new metric: the satisfaction frequency ψ (psi, i.e, the share of questions answered with precision and recall of at least 70% or an f1 of at least 60%). ψ ranks systems the same way precision, recall and f1 — a machine learning metric built from the harmonic mean of precision and recall — but is easier to read and assess for humans. System architecture had a large effect: with full use of Claude Opus 4.8 the plain document RAG of our earlier GNQA system had a ψ of 36% against 86% for our new combined tools. Delegating most of the work from Claude Opus 4.8 to a local model halved query costs while still reaching a ψ of 59%.

title: Datura: Progressive Red Teaming Testing for Tool Invocation Chain in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents that invoke external tools face critical safety vulnerabilities when malicious manipulations exploit their implicit trust in tool outputs and metadata. However, identifying these vulnerabilities through testing is challenging due to the need to bypass safety guardrails with semantically legitimate inputs, the difficulty in characterizing successful attacks amid implicit tool trust, and the requirement to maintain logical consistency across fragile state-dependent execution chains. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical study to investigate how external tools influence agent reasoning. Guided by the findings, we propose Datura, an automated red teaming testing framework that exposes safety vulnerabilities through chained tool manipulation. Through a five-stage workflow, Datura dynamically generates test cases where each individual step appears legitimate yet collectively leads to harmful outcomes. We evaluate Datura across five LLMs and 740 safety-critical tasks under five defense settings, including real-world safety mechanisms. Under Model Alignment, Datura achieves 94.86--99.59% attack success rate (ASR), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 25.27 percentage points. Under Prompt Refuge, Datura maintains 78.78--95.54% ASR, showing that progressive tool-chain manipulation remains effective even under prompt-level safeguards.

title: On Limits of AI-Empowered Science: Mapping Creative Scientific Reasoning of Large Language Models
abstract: This paper investigates the creative reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) in scientific research, examining whether these systems can generate genuinely novel hypotheses or are limited to optimising existing knowledge. Using Boden’s framework of creativity (combinatorial, exploratory, and transformational), I develop a theoretical model that positions abductive and analogical reasoning as fundamental processes underlying creative scientific thinking. The framework distinguishes between selective abduction (choosing from pre-established hypotheses) and creative abduction (generating novel explanations through analogical mapping). Based on this framing, I review existing literature on LLM performance in abductive and analogical reasoning tasks. The fact of the matter is that while LLMs demonstrate proficiency in selective abduction, they are limited in their creative abductive reasoning and exhibit brittleness in analogical reasoning when faced with novel permutations. Therefore, I argue that current LLMs seem to be constrained to combinatorial and exploratory creativity rather than transformational creativity, even in the near future. Consequently, LLMs are likely to function primarily as assistants in iterative scientific research, helping optimise existing methodologies and solutions rather than fundamentally transforming scientific paradigms. The paper argues for a more rigorous process-based evaluation of LLM reasoning capabilities beyond accuracy metrics to understand their potential contributions to scientific discovery better.

title: Creative thinking in humans and artificial intelligence: A comparative review of neural, molecular, and social mechanisms.
abstract: Creative thinking drives the generation of novel and useful ideas, contributing to scientific progress and the resolution of social challenges. Evidence from the earliest stone tools, dating to approximately 3.3 million years ago, suggests that creativity among hominin ancestors played a key role in the emergence of human culture and civilization. Although creativity arises from brain activity, the underlying molecular mechanisms and neural substrates remain incompletely understood. Neurotransmitters involved in motivation, reward, and mood play crucial roles in promoting creative processes. Recent advances in high-resolution brain imaging have begun to identify both specific brain regions and large-scale neural networks associated with creative thinking. Meanwhile, rapid developments in artificial intelligence (AI) raise questions about whether machines can exhibit forms of creativity once considered uniquely human. The integration of large language models, multimodal learning, and next-generation computing technologies, including quantum computing, may substantially expand the capabilities of AI systems. Simultaneously, these technological advances are generating new insights and discussions about the characteristics and limitations of human intellectual activity, thereby underscoring the importance of creativity. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the molecular, neural, and social dimensions of creative thinking, compares the underlying characteristics of human and artificial creativity, and discusses how interactions between biological and AI may shape the future of creativity in the era of human-AI coexistence.

title: Large language model multiagent systems for industrial problem discovery and prioritization
abstract: A persistent gap separates academic research priorities from the operational challenges faced by manufacturing firms. Established identification methods, among them Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) workshops, Lean audits and consultant engagements, are episodic, bounded by participant expertise and organised along departmental lines, which makes cross-departmental issues hard to surface. Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) have meanwhile shown collaborative problem-solving ability in software engineering and, more recently, in shopfloor scheduling and supply chain coordination. This article is a Perspective. It develops a framework and a research agenda; implementation and empirical evaluation fall outside its scope and are set out as its first research priorities. Three contributions are offered. The first is a synthesis of literature from industrial problem identification, LLM-based autonomous agents and manufacturing AI, which positions the proposal against existing industrial LLM agent work. The second is a framework in which six domain-specialised agents (production, quality, maintenance, supply chain, safety, energy) would collaborate through a five-phase protocol: worker-driven discovery, cross-departmental analysis, candidate-relationship detection, consensus-based financial assessment and debate-driven prioritisation. The prioritisation procedure is fully specified, including the normalisation of financial estimates, a measure of estimate dispersion, the derivation of criteria weights, a non-compensatory gate for safety-critical items and a mandatory human verification step. The third is a worked calculation on a hypothetical steel manufacturing vignette, included so that the procedure can be reproduced and scrutinised rather than as evidence of effectiveness. A preliminary qualitative readiness assessment and a three-horizon agenda of fourteen research questions complete the paper. The benefits identified are presented as hypotheses for that agenda to test rather than as demonstrated outcomes.

title: Applications of Generative AI for Advancing Scientific Content Production, Evaluation and Dissemination
abstract: Generative AI is becoming part of how scientific content is being produced, evaluated and communicated. Large language models (LLMs) can write science news, simulate readers, retrieve evidence, generate scientific hypotheses, write code, and execute research workflows. These capabilities create opportunities for accelerating scientific discovery and broadening access to scientific information, but they also introduce risks related to hallucination and trustworthiness. This doctoral dissertation studies how generative AI can support scientific content production and dissemination, while preserving trust, comprehension, and replicability. The completed work includes three components: (1) detecting LLM-generated science news through SANews and GFS, (2) evaluating science communication through reader learning using KnowledgeGain and LLMSim, and (3) benchmarking LLM agents for research replication with ReplicatorBench and ReplicatorAgent. The proposed work extends these directions toward learning-optimized science news generation, MESH for multimodal evidence-grounded hypothesis generation, and MERIT, a simulation-grounded framework for evaluating autonomous AI co-scientists and hypothesis testing in computational materials discovery. The overarching goal is to develop evaluation methods and AI systems that make scientific outputs not only fluent and scalable, but also grounded, useful, and interpretable.

title: Memory Architectures for Game Agents: A Systematic Mapping Study Bridging Classical and LLM Paradigms
abstract: Introduction: Two decades of research on memory for game agents have produced two largely disjoint traditions: classical symbolic game AI (blackboards, GOAP, behavior trees, case-based reasoning, Soar/ACT-R) and LLM-based agents (memory streams, MemGPT, A-MEM, CoALA, Voyager). Despite clear conceptual overlap, no prior survey covers both under a unified lens for game agents. Objective: We bridge these traditions through a systematic mapping that classifies, compares, and identifies open problems across both paradigms. Methodology: Following Petersen et al.’s guidelines, we surveyed 113 works from 1972–2025 across ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and arXiv, with forward and backward snowballing on seminal anchors. Each work was coded along five axes: temporal horizon, representation, lifecycle operations, grounding target, and agent role. Results: The mapping yields (i) a unified five-axis taxonomy for both paradigms, (ii) empty cells exposing under-served combinations (notably crowd-agent memory and explicit forgetting), (iii) an integration lens identifying what LLM systems reinvent from classical game AI, what they add, and what they lose, and (iv) six open problems framing a research agenda for NPC memory.

title: The rise of agentic AI in drug discovery from static tools to autonomous virtual scientists
abstract: Driven by large language models, AI agents are transforming drug discovery, enabling AI to break free from task-specific tools and advance toward the vision of autonomous virtual scientists. This perspective reviews applications across the R&D lifecycle. To evaluate system maturity, we introduce a 6-level “Spectrum of Agentic Autonomy.” We advocate for novel evaluation paradigms centered on full-chain traceability and outline adoption barriers, positioning AI agents as pragmatic scientist-in-the-loop co-pilots.

title: Agentic artificial intelligence in mechanics of materials: A review of building tailored models on demand
abstract: In mechanics of materials, many powerful methods are accessible only to experts. Constitutive models, for example, describe the relation between stress and strain in materials and are a core ingredient of simulations from structural engineering to biomechanics. Yet building and using such models requires specialized expertise—a barrier for the many potential users trained in other fields. Artificial intelligence based on foundation models, increasingly organized as agents, is beginning to lower this barrier by allowing users to generate tailored models on demand. The same development is underway in many other fields where specialized tools have long been hand‐crafted anew for each task. We call this emerging paradigm the on‐the‐fly generation of physical models : from a plain request, an agent creates a physical model on demand—from scratch and tailored to the problem. Its appeal is accessibility and flexibility. As a consequence, the lasting artifact is no longer a fixed model but the orchestration and prompting of the agents that produce it. This review surveys the concepts behind the paradigm, within mechanics of materials and in neighboring fields, and examines them through two lenses: effectiveness (the accuracy of the generated models) and trustworthiness (their physical admissibility). Trustworthiness is pursued along two routes: deepening the agent's integration under explicit validation, or restraining its autonomy in favor of trusted components. Given the rapid progress of foundation models, and the bitter lesson that general methods leveraging computation tend to prevail, we call for paradigms designed to scale with this progress rather than to compete with it.

title: Autonomous Agents Based on Large Language Models: Reasoning Strategies and Multi-Agent Interaction
abstract: Language-model agents acquire capability along two routes that published work almost always varies together, one enlarging the computation a single agent performs and the other enlarging the number of agents and the channels along which they pass partial results, which leaves the contribution of each route indistinguishable. This paper separates an agent system into a reasoning operator and an interaction topology, holding the number of agents fixed at three across all multi-agent topologies, together with the number of rounds, the message cap, the prompt skeleton, and the memory settings for all combinations, and evaluates a full factorial design of four reasoning levels and four topologies on three public test sets totalling 484 instances under five random seeds, giving 38,720 task executions. Comparisons are paired at the instance level, and effects are estimated from logistic mixed-effects models fitted to each test set separately. The reasoning factor spans 18.0 points on the static suite whereas the topology factor spans 7.8 points on the interactive one, a reversal indicating that the two mechanisms act on different failure modes. The topology span is taken across all four topology levels and therefore includes the step from one agent to three, against a structure-only span of 2.8 points among the multi-agent topologies. The two factors also depart from additivity in a localised manner. A mechanism-motivated single-degree-of-freedom contrast on the only cell in which both factors contribute a corrective pass is significant at p = 0.001 on the static suite, whereas the omnibus nine-degree-of-freedom interaction test is not (p = 0.094), and in that cell the observed 50.0 percent lies 5.8 points below the additive expectation. After tokens are counted, seven of the sixteen configurations remain undominated on the static suite and five on the operating-system suite, and returns saturate at 12,400 tokens per instance on the static suite under the present design.
